Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : BM4771 : Biotransport Laboratory { 0-0-3 / 2}

Subject Nature : Practical

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module 1: Fluid Dynamics in Biological Systems: Introduction to biofluid mechanics, Viscosity and rheology of biological fluids, Experiments on flow in blood vessels (Poiseuille's law, pulsatile flow) and Rheological properties of blood.
Module 2: Mass Transport Phenomena: Diffusion and osmosis experiments, Mass transfer in biological membranes, Drug delivery systems: experiments with diffusion and permeation, Techniques for measuring concentration profiles.
Module 3: Heat Transfer in Biological Systems: Basics of biological heat transfer, Experimental setup for thermal conductivity in tissues, Transient thermal analysis: simulation vs. experiment and Temperature regulation in biological systems.
Module 4: Integrated Transport Applications: Combined heat and mass transfer experiments, Simulation and modeling of transport in organs (kidney, lung), Microfluidics for biological applications. Project on a specific application (drug release, and tissue engineering)

Course Objective

1 .

Gain a deep understanding of the principles of fluid, mass, and heat transport in biological systems.
2 .

Develop skills in designing, conducting, and analyzing transport-related experiments.
3 .

Learn to interpret experimental data to validate theoretical models and understand biological processes.
4 .

Apply transport phenomena principles to solve real-world biomedical problems.

Course Outcome

1 .

1. Demonstrate proficiency in conducting experiments related to bio transport.
2. Analyze and interpret experimental results, correlating them with theoretical predictions.
3. Validate transport models using experimental data, enhancing their understanding of biological systems.
4. Apply learned concepts to design experiments or systems that address specific biomedical challenges.

George A. Truskey, Fan Yuan, and David F. Katz, Transport Phenomena in Biological Systems, Pearson

6386.b:
Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : PH3001 : Thermal and Statistical Physics { 3-1-0 / 4}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module 1: (8 hours)
Basic Concept: Concept of thermodynamic state, Thermodynamic limit, The ideal gas, extensive and intensive variables. Heat and heat capacities, Concept of probability for continuous and discrete distributions, Zeroth law of thermodynamics and thermal equilibrium. Brief discussion on microstates, macrostates, and statistical definition of temperature. Qualitative idea of microcanonical, canonical ensembles. Boltzmann factor from canonical ensemble.
Module 2: (10 hours)
Kinetic theory and transport properties of gases: Maxwell-Boltzmann (MB) speed distribution and mean kinetic energy of an ideal gas, most probable velocity, pressure expression from kinetic theory, ideal gas law, molecular flux and effusion rate, Collision cross section, mean collision time and mean free path, coefficient of viscosity, thermal conductivity, thermal diffusion equation, Newton’s law of cooling.
Module 3: (12 hours)
Equilibrium and work: thermodynamic equilibrium, state function, definition of work, quasi-static, isobaric and isochoric processes, work in a hydrostatic system, isothermal compressibility. First law: statement of first law, heat capacity of an ideal and non-ideal gas, reversibility, isothermal expansion or compression of an ideal gas, adiabatic expansion of an ideal gas. Second law: various statements and equivalence, Carnot engine and theorem, heat engines, refrigerator, heat pump, Clausius’s theorem, definition of entropy, irreversible changes and entropy, Joule expansion. Entropy and probability.
Module 4: (4 hours)
Thermodynamic Potentials: Thermodynamic potentials, Helmholtz, Enthalpy, Gibbs, grand potential, Maxwell’s relations, stability of equilibrium state. Third law: Different statements of third law, consequences of third law.
Module 5: (12 hours)
Statistical Thermodynamics of classical systems: Equipartition theorem and application, partition function and function of the state, Density of states, Functions of state of the ideal gas, Gibbs paradox, Heat capacity of a diatomic gas, definition and meaning of chemical potential, Grand partition function and grand potential, Chemical potential and chemical reactions, Latent heat, chemical potential and phase changes, First order phase transition single component systems, Clausius-Clapeyeron equation, Phase diagram and Triple point, multicomponent systems, Gibbs phase rule, Classification of phase transitions. Thermodynamics of real gases. Radiation: Energy density and pressure of radiation, Blackbody radiation and Kirchhoff’s law, Blackbody (Cavity) radiation as a thermodynamic system.

Course Objective

1 .

To learn the fundamental aspects of thermodynamics, including thermodynamic systems and properties.
2 .

To learn the kinetic theory of gases and the transport phenomenon involved in ideal gases.
3 .

To learn the laws of thermodynamics along with the concepts of temperature, internal energy, heat, and entropy.
4 .

To learn the thermodynamic potentials and their physical interpretations.
5. To understand the foundation of statistical mechanics of ideal gas and classification of phase transitions.

Course Outcome

1 .

At the end of the course, students will be able to:
CO1: Explain the fundamental concepts relevant to thermodynamics.
CO2: Understand the basic aspects of the kinetic theory of gases, the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution law, and the transport phenomenon in ideal gases.
CO3: Gain knowledge on the first and the second law of thermodynamics, the concept of entropy, the working of Carnot’s ideal heat engine, Carnot cycle and its efficiency.
CO4: Develop the concept of thermodynamic potentials, the formulation of Maxwell’s equations and its applications.
CO5: Analyze the nature of phase transitions in terms of simple thermodynamic variables.

Essential Reading

1 .

M. W. Zemansky and R. Dittman, Heat and Thermodynamics, McGraw-Hill Ltd. , 7th Edition (2007).

2 .

S. J. Blundell and K. M. Blundell, Concepts in Thermal Physics, Oxford University Press , 2nd Edition (2010).

Supplementary Reading

1 .

H. B. Callen., Thermodynamics and an Introduction to Thermostatistics, John Wiley & Sons , 2nd Edition (2006).

2 .

L. B. Loeb, Kinetic Theory of Gases, Dover Publications Inc. , 3rd Edition (2004).

Subject {L-T-P / C} : EE3000 : Electrical Machines { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module I (6L) - Transformer: Single-phase Transformer: Review of EMF equation and equivalent circuit, phasor diagrams on lo-load and full-load, per-unit representation of transformer parameters, voltage regulation, losses and efficiency, OC and SC test, all-day efficiency, parallel operation of transformers.
Module II (7L)- Three-phase Transformer: Construction of various types, operating characteristics of star–star, star–delta, delta–star, delta–delta, open–delta connections, vector groups.
Module III (6L)- DC Motor: Review of emf and torque equations, classification, losses and efficiency, Swinburne’s test and Hopkinson’s test, torque /speed characteristics, and speed control of shunt and series motors.
Module IV (7L) - Induction Machine: Three-phase induction motor: Construction and principle of operation, equivalent circuit and phasor diagram, torque-slip characteristics, no-load and blocked-rotor test, starting and speed control.
Module V (4L)- Single-phase induction motor: Principle of operation, torque-slip characteristics, starting methods.
Module VI (8L)- Synchronous Machines: Constructional features, synchronous generators and motors, equivalent circuit and phasor diagram, power and torque characteristics, voltage regulation of non-salient pole alternators by synchronous impedance method, V-curve and inverted-V curve, starting of synchronous motors.

Course Objective

1 .

Understand the various types of dc and ac electrical machines.
2 .

Understand the operating principles, testing methods, and connections of transformers, dc machines, induction machines, and synchronous machines.
3 .

Performance analysis of transformers, dc machines, induction machines, and synchronous machines.
4 .

Understanding the concepts of starting, braking, and/or speed control dc machines, induction machines, and synchronous machines.

Course Outcome

1 .

1. Understanding the concepts of various types of electrical machines.
2. Determine the induced/back EMF and torque equations of different kinds of electrical machines.
3. Performance analysis of single-, and three-phase transformers and various types of rotating machines.
4. Determine the various characteristics of rotating electrical machines.
5. Investigate the various starting, braking, and/or speed control methods of rotating machines.

Subject {L-T-P / C} : PH6126 : Stellar Structure and Evolution { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module 1: Formation of stars, Initial Mass Function, Equation of State, Stellar Structure Equations, Pre-main sequence evolution, Hayashi Track, Zero Age Main Sequence, H-burning Phase, PP Chain, CNO Cycle,
Module 2: Energy Transportation in lower and upper main sequence stars, Criteria for the onset of convection, Mass Luminosity Relation, Virial theorem, Source of opacity in stellar medium, Effect of chemical composition on stellar evolution
Module 3: Overall Contraction Phase, H-burning in shell, Schönberg-Chandrasekhar limit, properties of subgiant and red-giant branch stars, Hertzsprung gap
Module 4: Onset of He-burning, Horizontal Branch stars, Asymptotic giant branch stars, Properties of Luminous Blue Variables and Wolf-Rayet stars, Planetary Nebula Phase, White dwarf, Chandrasekhar limit, C, Ne, O, Si - burning phases, Supernova explosion, formation of Neutron Star and Black hole.
Module 5: Probing the interior using stellar pulsation: Stellar Pulsation Across HR-diagram, pulsation mechanism, Pulsation Mode Identification, Modelling of stellar pulsation, generating rotation profile from pulsation.

Course Objective

1 .

To learn the basics of star formation and stellar structure.
2 .

To get acquainted with energy transportation in stars.
3 .

To understand the post-main sequence evolution and final fate of stars.
4 .

To develop the understanding of stellar pulsation and its application.

Course Outcome

1 .

(1) Students will understand the theory of star formation and early evolution.
(2) Students will acquire the knowledge to construct the models of stars.
(3) Students will understand the advance evolutionary status of stars
(4) Students will know the process of supernovae explosion and formation of neutron star & black hole
(5) Students will learn the methods to probe the interior of stars.
